title: How Numerology Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain numerology as a pseudo-scientific practice that assigns mystical meaning to numbers. They trace its roots to Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans in southern Italy (sacred numbers, figurate numbers, odd/even gender associations, the discovery of irrational numbers), its revival through nineteenth-century writers including Josephine Balliett's vibration-based books, and modern methods such as the name-based destiny number, the life path number from birth date, and the birth-day-only shortcut. They work through a sample calculation using Chuck's name, discuss confirmation bias, the made-up nature of base-ten counting, and the question of harm versus comfort, with a caveat about anti-science sentiment. The episode closes with a listener email about the annulli lizard in Georgia.

segments.title: Opening banter and shout-outs
segments.summary: The hosts joke about their numerology numbers, introduce the topic as a pseudoscientific practice, and share shout-outs to Matt Sweeney, listener Jimmy McCleod, and Flathead Lake cheese.

segments.title: Numerology's mystical basis and Pythagoras
segments.summary: The hosts describe the belief that numbers carry vibrations that govern life, and introduce Pythagoras as the father of Western numerology, including his musical harmony discoveries with hammers.

segments.title: Pythagorean theorem and the Pythagoreans' fall
segments.summary: The Pythagoreans made real mathematical advances, including the Pythagorean theorem and odd-number square patterns, but mystical claims grew. The school was sacked and burned in southern Italy, with at least fifty killed.

segments.title: Pythagorean number categories and sacred ten
segments.summary: The Pythagoreans sorted numbers into square, triangular, and oblong categories, assigned gender to odd and even numbers, called ten sacred, and listed ten fundamental opposites. They also identified perfect numbers such as six.

segments.title: Irrational numbers and the decline of the school
segments.summary: The discovery of irrational numbers, such as the square root of two, undermined the Pythagorean worldview. Mysticism faded after their deaths and was revived in the nineteenth century.

segments.title: Nineteenth-century revival and vibrations
segments.summary: Josephine Balliett's books in the 1800s promoted the idea that everything has a numeric vibration and that one's environment should match one's number. The hosts compare this to string theory and recall Pythagoras's music of the spheres.

segments.title: Modern numerology: name and birth numbers
segments.summary: Modern practice uses letter-to-number charts. The destiny (expression) number comes from the full birth name, and the life path number comes from the birth date. Chuck's name calculation yields seven, and both hosts have life path nines.

segments.title: Criticism, Harry Potter, confirmation bias, and harm
segments.summary: The hosts discuss numerology's links to Harry Potter and Tracy Wilson's article, birth-day-only shortcuts, confirmation bias, and the made-up nature of base-ten counting. They weigh harm against comfort and voice concern about anti-science sentiment. They close with the origin of the word eleven.

segments.title: Listener mail: the annulli lizard
segments.summary: Listener Cassie from Statesboro, Georgia writes that the lizard in the earlier short stuff episode on chameleons was an anole, not a gecko.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and invite listener mail, then sign off.
